notes:
Modern periodic law

Properties of elements are periodic functions of their atomic number (Moseley). The long form has 18 groups and 7 periods; period number = number of shells (value of $n$) of the outermost shell; elements in a group have similar valence-shell configuration.

Classification (block)

  • s-block: groups 1–2 (last electron enters s). p-block: groups 13–18. d-block (transition): groups 3–12. f-block (lanthanoids, actinoids).

Periodic trends

PropertyAlong a period (L→R)Down a group
Atomic radiusdecreases (↑ $Z_{eff}$)increases (new shell)
Ionic radiusdecreases (isoelectronic: more +ve charge → smaller)increases
Ionisation enthalpyincreasesdecreases
Electron gain enthalpybecomes more negative (exceptions: noble gases ~0)becomes less negative (Cl most negative, not F)
Electronegativityincreasesdecreases
Metallic characterdecreasesincreases

Exceptions & anomalies

  • IE: Be $>$ B, N $>$ O (extra stability of fully-filled 2s$^2$ and half-filled 2p$^3$).
  • Electron gain enthalpy of F is less negative than Cl due to F's small size and strong electron–electron repulsion in the compact 2p orbital.
  • Noble gases: IE maximum in their period; electron gain enthalpy ≈ 0 (stable octet).
  • Isoelectronic species (same electron count): radius decreases as nuclear charge increases, e.g. $N^{3-} > O^{2-} > F^- > Na^+ > Mg^{2+} > Al^{3+}$.

Diagonal relationship & anomalous behaviour

2nd period elements (Li, Be, B, C) resemble the diagonally placed 3rd period element of the next group (Li–Mg, Be–Al, B–Si) due to similar charge/size ratio. First member of each group often differs from the rest (e.g. Li, Be, B, C, N, O, F all show anomalous behaviour vs. their group).

Nomenclature

Elements with $Z > 100$ use IUPAC systematic names (nil=0, un=1, bi=2, tri=3, quad=4, pent=5, hex=6, sept=7, oct=8, enn=9), e.g. Z=104 → unnilquadium (Unq).

Exam tip

2–3 questions: ordering elements/ions by radius or IE, an anomaly question (Be>B, F vs Cl electron gain enthalpy), and an isoelectronic-species comparison. Learn the trend table cold — most questions are direct applications.

questions.q: The modern periodic law states that the properties of elements are a periodic function of their
questions.explanation: Moseley showed atomic number (nuclear charge), not atomic mass, correctly orders elements and predicts periodicity.
questions.trick: Modern periodic law: properties are periodic in atomic number, not atomic mass.

questions.q: Across a period from left to right, atomic radius generally
options: decreases due to increasing effective nuclear charge
questions.explanation: Electrons are added to the same shell while nuclear charge increases, pulling electrons closer and shrinking the radius.
questions.trick: Same shell, rising nuclear pull → radius shrinks left to right.

questions.q: Which order of first ionisation enthalpy is correct?
questions.explanation: Be has a stable, fully-filled 2s$^2$ configuration, making it harder to remove an electron than from B (2s$^2$2p$^1$), where the p-electron is easily lost.
questions.trick: Filled 2s$^2$ (Be) resists electron loss more than a lone 2p$^1$ (B).

questions.q: The electron gain enthalpy of chlorine is more negative than that of fluorine because
options: F's small size causes strong inter-electronic repulsion in the compact 2p subshell
Cl has a larger nuclear charge
questions.explanation: Despite F being more electronegative, its very small atomic size leads to significant electron-electron repulsion when an extra electron is added, making the process less exothermic than for Cl.
questions.trick: Small F → extra e–e repulsion in compact 2p → less exothermic than Cl.

questions.q: Among the following, the smallest radius is shown by
questions.explanation: All are isoelectronic (10 electrons); radius decreases as nuclear charge increases: $F^- > Na^+ > Mg^{2+} > Al^{3+}$.
questions.trick: Isoelectronic set: more nuclear charge → smaller radius; pick highest $Z$.

questions.q: The element with the highest electronegativity is
questions.explanation: Fluorine has the highest electronegativity (Pauling scale ≈ 4.0) of all elements.
questions.trick: Fluorine tops electronegativity on the Pauling scale — pure recall.

questions.q: Which element shows a diagonal relationship with lithium?
questions.explanation: Li (group 1, period 2) and Mg (group 2, period 3) have similar charge/size ratios, giving similar chemical properties (diagonal relationship).
questions.trick: Diagonal pairs: Li–Mg, Be–Al, B–Si (similar charge/size ratio).

questions.q: Elements are classified into s, p, d and f blocks based on
options: the number of valence electrons only
the subshell being filled by the last (differentiating) electron
questions.explanation: The block is decided by the subshell (s, p, d or f) into which the last electron enters according to the Aufbau principle.
questions.trick: Block = subshell (s/p/d/f) receiving the last (differentiating) electron.

questions.q: Which of the following has the largest atomic radius?
questions.explanation: Down group 17, a new shell is added at each step, so atomic radius increases: F < Cl < Br < I.
questions.trick: Down a group, new shell added each step → radius increases.

questions.q: Among the period-3 elements Na, Mg, Al and Ar, the correct order of first ionisation enthalpy is
questions.explanation: General trend is increasing IE across a period, but Al (3s$^2$3p$^1$) dips below Mg (stable 3s$^2$) because its lone p-electron is easily removed; overall order: Na < Al < Mg < Ar.
questions.trick: Al dips below Mg (lone p-electron); overall still Na < Al < Mg < Ar.

questions.q: Noble gases have very high ionisation enthalpies because
options: they have small atomic size only
they have completely filled stable electronic configurations
questions.explanation: A fully-filled octet ($ns^2np^6$) is extremely stable, so removing an electron requires very high energy.
questions.trick: Fully-filled octet ($ns^2np^6$) resists electron removal → highest IE in period.

questions.q: The systematic (IUPAC) name for the element with atomic number 104 is
questions.explanation: 1-0-4 → un-nil-quad-ium = unnilquadium (symbol Unq), following IUPAC digit roots (1=un, 0=nil, 4=quad).
questions.trick: IUPAC digit roots: 1=un, 0=nil, 4=quad → 104 = unnilquadium.

questions.q: Going down a group, metallic character generally
questions.explanation: Down a group atomic size increases and ionisation enthalpy decreases, so atoms lose electrons more easily — metallic character increases.
questions.trick: Down a group: bigger atom, lower IE → easier electron loss → more metallic.

questions.q: Which pair correctly represents an isoelectronic species pair?
questions.explanation: O$^{2-}$ (10 electrons) and F$^-$ (10 electrons) are isoelectronic; Na$^+$ (10) and Cl$^-$ (18) are not.
questions.trick: Isoelectronic = same electron count; check electrons, not just charge sign.

questions.q: The period number of an element in the modern periodic table corresponds to the
options: principal quantum number of the outermost shell
questions.explanation: Period number equals the value of $n$ (principal quantum number) of the outermost occupied shell.
questions.trick: Period number = principal quantum number $n$ of the outermost shell.

questions.q: Which of the following statements about electron gain enthalpy is correct?
options: Noble gases have a large positive electron gain enthalpy
It becomes more negative across a period generally
It decreases down a group without exception
questions.explanation: Across a period, increasing nuclear charge makes electron gain enthalpy more negative (more exothermic), with exceptions at noble gases and group 15.
questions.trick: Electron gain enthalpy generally turns more negative across a period.

questions.q: Which of the following elements belongs to the d-block?
questions.explanation: Sc (Z=21) has configuration [Ar]3d$^1$4s$^2$; the last electron enters the 3d subshell, placing it in the d-block.
questions.trick: d-block member: last electron enters (n−1)d, as in Sc's 3d$^1$4s$^2$.

questions.q: The first ionisation enthalpy of nitrogen is higher than that of oxygen because
options: nitrogen has a smaller atomic radius
nitrogen has a half-filled, extra-stable 2p$^3$ configuration
questions.explanation: A half-filled p-subshell (2p$^3$) has extra symmetry/exchange stability, making it harder to remove an electron from N than from O (2p$^4$), which has one paired, easily-lost electron.
questions.trick: Half-filled 2p$^3$ in N is extra stable → higher IE than O's 2p$^4$.

questions.q: Among Li, Na, K and Rb, the element with the highest ionisation enthalpy is
questions.explanation: Ionisation enthalpy decreases down group 1 as atomic size increases; Li, at the top, has the highest value.
questions.trick: IE decreases down a group; the topmost element (Li) has the highest.

questions.q: Which of the following ionic radii order is correct?
questions.explanation: For the same element, a higher positive charge means fewer electrons and greater effective nuclear pull per electron, so $Fe^{3+}$ is smaller than $Fe^{2+}$.
questions.trick: Same element, higher charge, fewer electrons → smaller ion: $Fe^{3+}<Fe^{2+}$.

questions.q: Mendeleev's periodic law stated that properties of elements are a periodic function of their
questions.explanation: Mendeleev arranged elements by increasing atomic mass; this was later corrected to atomic number by Moseley's modern periodic law.
questions.trick: Mendeleev used atomic mass; Moseley later corrected it to atomic number.

questions.q: The modern long-form periodic table has
questions.explanation: The long form of the periodic table has 18 vertical groups and 7 horizontal periods.
questions.trick: Long-form table: 18 groups × 7 periods — pure recall.

questions.q: A well-known consequence of lanthanoid contraction is that
options: atomic radii increase steadily across the lanthanoids
Zr and Hf have almost identical atomic radii
questions.explanation: The steady contraction in size across the lanthanoids means Hf (following the lanthanoids) has nearly the same radius as Zr, its 4d congener, making their chemistry very similar.
questions.trick: Lanthanoid contraction makes Zr and Hf nearly identical in size.

questions.q: Which of the following statements is correct regarding atomic and ionic radii?
options: an anion is smaller than its parent atom
a cation is smaller than its parent atom
an anion is always smaller than the corresponding cation
a cation is always larger than its parent atom
questions.explanation: Removing electrons increases effective nuclear charge per electron and often reduces shells, so a cation is always smaller than its parent atom; anions, gaining electrons, are larger.
questions.trick: Losing electrons shrinks an atom (cation); gaining electrons enlarges it (anion).

questions.q: Elements of which group typically show a common valency of 3 (in their hydrides/halides)?
questions.explanation: Group 15 elements (N, P, As...) have 5 valence electrons and commonly show a valency of 3 (e.g. NH$_3$, PCl$_3$).
questions.trick: Group 15 has 5 valence electrons → typical valency of 3 (e.g. NH$_3$).

questions.q: The correct order of increasing atomic radius among C, N, O and F is
questions.explanation: Across period 2, atomic radius decreases left to right (Li > Be > B > C > N > O > F), so the increasing order is F < O < N < C.
questions.trick: Radius falls left to right in a period; just reverse the period order.

questions.q: Which of the following oxides is amphoteric?
questions.explanation: Al$_2$O$_3$ reacts with both acids and bases, making it amphoteric, unlike the basic Na$_2$O/MgO or acidic SO$_3$.
questions.trick: Amphoteric oxide reacts with both acid and base — Al$_2$O$_3$ is the classic one.

questions.q: The correct order of increasing acidic character of the oxides Na$_2$O, MgO, Al$_2$O$_3$ and SiO$_2$ is
questions.explanation: Across period 3, oxide character changes from strongly basic (Na$_2$O) to basic (MgO) to amphoteric (Al$_2$O$_3$) to acidic (SiO$_2$), so acidic character increases in this order.
questions.trick: Period 3 oxides: basic → amphoteric → acidic left to right.

questions.q: Among Li, Na, K and Cs, the element with the highest metallic character is
questions.explanation: Metallic character increases down a group as ionisation enthalpy decreases; Cs, at the bottom of group 1, is the most metallic.
questions.trick: Metallic character rises down a group; the bottom-most element wins.

questions.q: Regarding electron gain enthalpy of oxygen and sulphur, which statement is correct?
options: S has a more negative electron gain enthalpy than O
neither has a negative electron gain enthalpy
O has a more negative electron gain enthalpy than S
questions.explanation: Like F vs Cl, the smaller O atom has greater electron-electron repulsion when gaining an electron, so S (larger, less repulsion) has a more negative electron gain enthalpy than O.
questions.trick: Smaller atom → more e–e repulsion on gaining e– → O less negative than S.

questions.q: Among the period-3 elements Na, Mg, Al and Si, the largest atomic radius is shown by
questions.explanation: Atomic radius decreases across a period due to increasing effective nuclear charge; Na, being leftmost, has the largest radius.
questions.trick: Leftmost element in a period has the largest atomic radius.

questions.q: The drop in ionisation enthalpy on going from group 2 to group 13 across a period (e.g. Mg to Al) is mainly due to
options: extra shielding provided by inner d-electrons
the added electron entering a p-orbital, which is less penetrating and more easily removed than an s-electron
a sharp increase in atomic size
a sudden decrease in nuclear charge
questions.explanation: The outermost electron in group 13 elements occupies a p-orbital, which is shielded by the filled s-orbital and is easier to remove than an s-electron, lowering ionisation enthalpy relative to group 2.
questions.trick: New p-electron is more shielded/penetrates less than s → IE drops at group 13.

questions.q: Among Na, Mg, Al and Si, the element with the highest first ionisation enthalpy is
questions.explanation: Actual IE$_1$ values (kJ mol$^{-1}$): Na 496, Al 578, Mg 738, Si 786. Despite the Mg–Al dip, Si (further right, with an increasing effective nuclear charge) has the highest IE$_1$ of this set.
questions.tip: Don't assume the period trend is perfectly monotonic across group boundaries — check actual anomalies at groups 2→13 and 15→16.
questions.trick: Don't assume smooth trend across group 2–13; check actual IE values when unsure.

questions.q: The total number of elements present in period 2 of the periodic table is
questions.explanation: Period 2 runs from Li (Z=3) to Ne (Z=10), containing 8 elements.
questions.trick: Period 2 runs Li to Ne — just count the elements: 8.

questions.q: Transition (d-block) elements commonly show variable oxidation states mainly because of
options: the small energy difference between (n-1)d and ns orbitals, allowing both to participate in bonding
high melting points of transition metals
questions.explanation: Since (n-1)d and ns orbitals are close in energy, a variable number of d-electrons (in addition to ns electrons) can be lost, giving multiple oxidation states.
questions.trick: Close (n−1)d/ns energy gap lets variable electron loss → variable oxidation states.

questions.q: The correct decreasing order of ionic radius for the isoelectronic species O$^{2-}$, F$^-$, Na$^+$ and Mg$^{2+}$ is
questions.explanation: All four species have 10 electrons; radius decreases as nuclear charge increases: O(Z=8) < F(Z=9) < Na(Z=11) < Mg(Z=12), so O$^{2-}$ > F$^-$ > Na$^+$ > Mg$^{2+}$.
questions.trick: Isoelectronic (10 e–): higher nuclear charge → smaller ion; rank by $Z$.

questions.q: The lanthanoid elements are placed in period
questions.explanation: Lanthanoids (Ce to Lu, Z=58–71) belong to period 6, following La.
questions.trick: Lanthanoids (Z=58–71) sit in period 6, right after La.

questions.q: Actinoid contraction is more pronounced than lanthanoid contraction mainly because
options: 5f electrons are core electrons in all actinoids
actinoids have a lower nuclear charge
4f orbitals shield the nuclear charge poorly
5f orbitals shield the nuclear charge even more poorly than 4f orbitals
questions.explanation: The diffuse 5f orbitals shield the nuclear charge even less effectively than 4f orbitals, so the effective nuclear charge increases more sharply across the actinoids, causing greater contraction.
questions.trick: 5f orbitals shield even worse than 4f → actinoid contraction is sharper.

questions.q: The correct order of increasing first ionisation enthalpy for P, S, Cl and Ar is
questions.explanation: S dips below P because P's half-filled 3p$^3$ is extra stable (like N vs O), so the actual order is S < P < Cl < Ar, not the naively expected monotonic increase.
questions.trick: Half-filled 3p$^3$ in P is extra stable → S dips below P in IE.

questions.q: The tendency of a bonded atom to attract the shared pair of electrons towards itself is called
questions.explanation: This attracting tendency within a covalent bond defines electronegativity, distinct from electron affinity (a property of an isolated gaseous atom).
questions.trick: Attraction for a shared bonding pair defines electronegativity, not electron affinity.
